analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage insurers to disclose denied claims, prior authorizations, and benefit spending, with payment cuts for noncompliance.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees on September 28, 2022, and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force private Medicare Advantage insurers to tell the government, in standardized form, what they actually deliver: how much they spend on the extra benefits they advertise, how many claims they deny and why, how often they require prior approval before care, and which doctors are really in their networks. Plans that fail to submit complete data would see their Medicare payments cut by 5 to 10 percent per month until they comply, and repeat offenders could have claims processed directly by Medicare contractors instead. It is a transparency and enforcement bill aimed at an insurance industry that receives roughly half of all Medicare spending while reporting little about how it uses the money.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in or considering Medicare Advantage plans — roughly half of all Medicare recipients — would get plain-language, verifiable information about the supplemental benefits plans advertise, the doctors actually in each network, and how often plans deny care or make patients wait for prior approval. Medicare officials and Congress would gain the data needed to catch insurers that overstate benefits or overbill, and taxpayers would benefit if payment accuracy improved as a result. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Requires every Medicare Advantage plan to report, within 6 months of each plan year, standardized data on its supplemental benefits: how many enrollees have access to each benefit, how many actually used it, what the plan and beneficiaries spent, and all related claims data — so advertised perks can be checked against reality.

Requires plans to report the number of claims denied and by what reason, the number of prior-authorization requests, how long patients waited between approval and care, how often denials and prior authorizations were appealed and overturned, and how often inpatient stays were converted to cheaper outpatient status.

Requires the government to publish the encounter data it receives and to keep an up-to-date (at least quarterly) public listing of which providers and suppliers are in each plan's network and whether they are accepting new patients.

Backs the requirements with teeth: a plan missing supplemental-benefit data loses 5 percent of its Medicare payment each month until it complies; a plan that submits no encounter data loses 10 percent per month; incomplete or inaccurate data triggers a Secretary-determined cut of up to 5 percent; and plans with bad data two years running must let Medicare contractors process claims directly.
Shifts quality star ratings toward the plan level rather than the contract level, making it harder for an insurer to average out one bad plan's performance under a large contract.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurance companies — including the large national carriers that dominate the program — bear the cost: they must build standardized reporting systems, hand over claims and denial data they currently keep private, and face monthly payment reductions of 5 to 10 percent for incomplete or missing submissions. Some of that cost could ultimately reach taxpayers and enrollees if insurers respond by trimming supplemental benefits or exiting plans, though the bill's purpose is precisely to test whether advertised benefits are real.

drawbacks.text: The bill only counts and publishes denials, prior authorizations, and wait times — it does not ban any denial practice or speed up approvals, so beneficiaries could learn more about being refused care without that care getting any easier to obtain.

The financial penalties are sizable and mechanical: 5 to 10 percent of a plan's monthly Medicare payment is a large sum, and insurers could respond by dropping plans, narrowing supplemental benefits, or raising cost sharing to offset the risk — costs that would land on enrollees.

Compliance hinges on future rulemaking: the Secretary must define the metrics for 'complete and accurate' data, the denial code categories, and the incompleteness levels, so how tough the law is in practice depends entirely on the administration carrying it out.
The reporting burden is substantial and extends to third-party contractors that provide supplemental benefits, which adds administrative cost across the industry in the first years of implementation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are information and enforcement leverage; its costs are administrative burden on insurers and possible payment cuts that could ripple into plan offerings. For beneficiaries, knowing that a heavily advertised benefit is rarely used, or that a plan denies a high share of claims, is genuinely valuable in choosing coverage — and taxpayers have a direct stake in whether encounter data shows insurers are coding their way to higher payments. The main design weakness is that the bill sheds light on problems rather than fixing them directly, and its strength depends on later regulations; but the payment penalties and the escalation to direct claims processing give it more than typical transparency-bill teeth. The burden falls on an industry that already receives large public payments, which is where an accountability measure of this kind would expect to place it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and a subcommittee the day after it was introduced, and it sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Katie Porter introduced the bill on September 28, 2022, joined by nine Democratic cosponsors including Diana DeGette, Lloyd Doggett, Jan Schakowsky, Mark Pocan, and Pramila Jayapal.
The same day, the House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, the two panels that share jurisdiction over Medicare.
The next day, September 29, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action of any kind was ever recorded.
Neither committee held a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, which automatically killed it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers are better off: they never had to disclose their denial, prior-authorization, and supplemental-benefit data publicly, and they avoided the 5 to 10 percent monthly payment cuts the bill imposed for incomplete reporting.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; all 10 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, so the bill never tested whether it had support beyond one party.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers to disclose claims denials, prior-authorization practices, supplemental-benefit spending, and full encounter data, and would cut their Medicare payments 5 to 10 percent per month for incomplete reporting. Insurers' interest in keeping that data private runs directly against beneficiaries' interest in knowing what they are buying and what care is being refused.

Companies that insurers hire to provide dental, vision, and other supplemental benefits would be contractually required to submit the same standardized spending and utilization data to the government, adding reporting obligations they do not currently face.
